prs.title: fix(app-render): stop prerendered Link headers from accumulating on revalidation
prs.author: linyiru
prs.body:
### What?

With `cacheComponents: true`, a `Link` header set in `next.config.js` `headers()` (or by middleware) is duplicated on ISR pages that also emit a React preload `Link` (e.g. an ``), and gains one more copy on every background revalidation:

```
req 3  Link: </llms.txt>; rel="llms-txt"
       Link: </llms.txt>; rel="llms-txt",</llms.txt>; rel="llms-txt",</hero.png>; rel=preload; as="image"; fetchpriority="high"
req 4  Link: </llms.txt>; rel="llms-txt"
       Link: </llms.txt>; rel="llms-txt",</llms.txt>; rel="llms-txt",</llms.txt>; rel="llms-txt",</hero.png>; rel=preload; ...
...
```

An on-demand render (cache `MISS`) of a page not prerendered at build time also returns both the config `Link` and the preload `Link` twice.

### Why?

`prerenderToStream` handles React's `onHeaders` by appending each value to the live response and then storing `res.getHeader(name)` in `metadata.headers`, which becomes the APP_PAGE cache entry's `headers`. That snapshot includes values the render did not produce:

- the `Link` from `headers()` in next.config.js, already on the response before rendering;
- during a background revalidation, the `Link` values the serving path replayed from the previous cache entry onto the same response.

`app-page-runtime` appends the cache entry's headers to every response after the config headers are set, so each regeneration stores, and later serves, one more copy. On a `MISS` the render has already written the headers to the response, and the same valu

prs.title: Turbopack: replace Next.js entry kinds with an opaque entry tag
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
## Summary

`EntryReferenceSubType` in turbopack-core listed Next.js concepts: pages, data routes, API routes, middleware, instrumentation, client components and others. Most of them were only ever constructed, and nothing read which one it was. Two places did read them, both in Next.js:

- The pages router rule that strips the default export from a page's data route matched `PageData`.
- `create_page_ssr_entry_module` chose its route template by decoding `Page`, `PageData` or `PagesApi` from the reference type it was given.

This came up in review of #101152. That PR needs Turbopack to treat page entries differently, and would otherwise match on these variants in the `turbopack` crate.

`EntryReferenceSubType` is now a struct with a `tag` that the embedder defines and Turbopack doesn't interpret. `ReferenceTypeCondition::Entry` matches on that tag. Next.js tags the data route entry with `next-page-data`. A new `PagesEntryKind` (`Page`, `Data`, `Api`) is passed to `create_page_ssr_entry_module` and decides both the template and the reference type. All other entries use the untagged default.

No behavior change is intended. Entries that differed only by a variant nobody read may now share a `process` task.

## Verification

- `cargo check -p next-api -p turbopack-cli -p turbopack-node -p turbopack-tests --tests` has no warnings.
- `cargo nextest r -p turbopack-core -p turbopack-tests` passes, with no snapshot changes.

prs.title: Turbopack: don't split page entries into a facade
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
## Summary

Fixes an HMR bug in the Pages Router with Turbopack. When an edit added or removed a re-export in a page, Fast Refresh reported the update as done, but the page kept showing the old content until a later edit forced a full reload. Webpack does a full reload in this case.

With `follow_reexports`, whether a module has re-exports decides whether it is split into a facade and its locals module. For a page entry, an edit that added a re-export therefore changed the module the page entry points at. HMR doesn't follow that change.

Page entries are now never split. Next.js marks pages router entries `standalone`, a new property of `EntryReferenceSubType` (#101291 removed the Next.js entry kinds from turbopack-core). Turbopack keeps a standalone entry whole: it doesn't follow its reexports and doesn't split it into a facade or into module fragments, since either would make its identity depend on its reexports. Nothing imports a page entry's exports, so there is nothing to tree-shake. This is limited to page entries. Other entries, such as client components, are also imported by other modules. Those imports would still be split, so the module would be evaluated twice.

A stack in the dev overlay loses the extra frame the facade added (`ReactRefreshLogBox` "module init error not shown").

This PR first removed `HmrEntryModule` too, but it is still needed. The page loader's ident includes the page's ident, so renaming a page, e.g. from `.js` to `.tsx` (`test/development/typ
…(truncated)

prs.title: Turbopack: use hash collections for turbo-tasks values whose order is unobserved
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
## Summary

Follow-up to #100935. `IndexMap`/`IndexSet` compare like a map/set, ignoring order, and a turbo-tasks cell keeps its old content when the recomputed value is equal. So a value whose order matters can silently keep a stale order. To make it obvious which collections don't care about order, this switches turbo-tasks value fields whose order is never observed to hash collections. Their consumers only look entries up, or iterate into results that don't depend on order.

Changed:
- `StyleGroups.shared_chunk_items`, `VisitedModules.modules`, `ExcludedExtensions`, `FontData`, `FontMetricsMap` → `FxHashMap`/`FxHashSet`
- `RouteTree.static_segments` → `FrozenMap`: fixed once the tree is built, and kept sorted so `to_string`, equality and serialization stay deterministic
- The tag-keyed maps in the browser and Node.js chunking contexts (`client_roots`, `asset_root_paths`, `asset_base_paths`/`asset_prefixes`, `url_behaviors`) → `AutoMap`, since they hold a handful of tags

Left as `IndexMap`/`IndexSet`, because their iteration order reaches batching, idents, generated code, manifests or nft output:
- `CollectedModules`, `OutputAssetsSet`/`OutputAssetsMap`, `InnerAssets`, `Project.additional_roots`, `CollectedRootParams`, the env maps, `EnvVarInfo.runtime`, and the cache-handler, modularize-imports and tracing config maps
- `CompileTimeDefines`/`FreeVarReferences` never read their order, but look entries up with borrowed segment keys through `Equivalent`, which `HashMap` does
…(truncated)

prs.title: Bump `is-animated@3.0.19`
prs.author: styfle
prs.body:
## Summary

Bumps `is-animated` from 2.0.2 to 3.0.19 and refreshes the vendored bundle and preserves CJS export now that upstream ships ESM.

## Performance

A local detection-only benchmark across 9 existing image fixtures measured 33–34% less detection time for an equally weighted mix: approximately 1.09 → 0.73 µs per call. This reproduced in two runs with 24 alternating A/B pairs per fixture on an Apple M3 Pro using Node.js 26.12.1, with buffers loaded before timing.

Results vary by format: animated GIF detection took about 38% less time, and the two animated PNG fixtures took 11–82% less time. Animated WebP took about 0.16 µs longer per call; static PNG, JPEG, and AVIF detection also took longer.

End-to-end image optimization was not benchmarked since these are µs improvements.

- Related to https://github.com/FRSOURCE/is-animated/pull/49

prs.title: turbopack-ecmascript: store AstPathTrie nodes as parent and kind indices
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
## Summary

`AstPathTrie` nodes stored their `AstParentKind` inline: a 4-byte parent index plus the 24-byte kind (swc's outer node type, inner field, and a `usize` index for list fields), padded to 32 bytes. The tries live in the `CodeGens` cell of every analyzed module, so they are kept for the rest of the build.

Each trie now stores its distinct kinds once, in a table, and a node is two `u32`s: its parent and the index of its kind, 8 bytes. Most kinds repeat throughout a module (`Expr::Call`, `CallExpr::Callee`, ...); only the indexed ones (statement and argument positions) tend to be distinct. The builder interns kinds with an `FxIndexSet` and keys its children maps by the 4-byte kind index; the trie's API is unchanged.

### Results

Large Next.js app, cold `next build --experimental-build-mode=compile`, live heap sampled at the end of the build:

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AstPathTrie`s | 701 MiB (~23M nodes) | 269 MiB |
| Live heap | 13.55 GiB | 13.11 GiB |
| User CPU | 504–514 s | 506 s |

About 18% of nodes have a distinct kind, so the table costs ~94 MiB and the nodes ~175 MiB. The tries are serialized with the `CodeGens` cell, so the persistent cache shrinks too.

## Verification

- `cargo nextest r -p turbopack-ecmascript`
- `cargo nextest r -p turbopack-tests` (snapshot tests compare generated code, so path lookups produce identical output)

prs.title: turbo-tasks-backend: release unused capacity in task storage
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
## Summary

Task storage held more memory than its contents need because several of its collections never give capacity back:

- **The lazy field vec** (`TinyVec<LazyField>`) is shrunk to fit after each execution, but every field another task adds to a finished task later (cell dependents, aggregation edges, dirty state) doubled its capacity again. At the end of a large build it held ~1.75 slots per entry. Lazy fields are now pushed with `TinyVec::push_exact`, which grows by one slot, and `TinyVec` resizes heap buffers with `realloc` so the allocator can keep blocks in place.
- **Aggregation edges** (`upper`, `followers`, the aggregated dirty/collectible counters) move around constantly while the aggregation graph rebalances, and neither hash tables nor spilled lists shrink on their own, so they kept their peak capacity: `followers`' hash tables held 4.8x the bytes of their entries. `CounterMap` now calls `shrink_amortized` after removing entries, which shrinks once capacity exceeds 3x the length (3x rather than 2x, because a table right after doubling is already at ~2x).
- **Emptied lazy collections** kept an empty `LazyField` (137K empty `followers` on a large build). The generated `CounterMap` mutators now drop the field when it becomes empty, checked with an O(1) `is_empty` on the map they already hold; removing a lazy field shrinks the vec once at most half of it is used.

### Results

Large Next.js app (front `vercel-site`, 7.9M tasks), cold `next build --experimental-b

prs.title: Turbopack: support turbopackIgnore on new URL()
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
## Summary

A user reported that `next build` fails on `new URL(options.workerUrl, import.meta.url)` inside a branch that only runs when the caller passes a worker URL. The analyzer sees the URL as `(<dynamic> | 'undefined')` and fails with `Module not found: Can't resolve (<dynamic> | 'undefined')`, and there was no way to mark the URL as runtime-only.

- `new URL()` now honors the same magic comments as `new Worker()`. `new URL(/* turbopackIgnore: true */ url, import.meta.url)` (or `webpackIgnore`) creates no asset reference and is left as-is in the output, so the URL resolves at runtime. `turbopackOptional` suppresses the resolve error. The Turbopack docs list `new URL()` with the other supported expressions.
- When a partially dynamic `new URL()`, `import()` or `require()` fails to resolve, the "Module not found" message suggests the matching `turbopackIgnore` comment. This adds a line to the existing `require()` warning in `execution/turbopack/resolving/dynamic`.

Resolution behavior is otherwise unchanged: a partially dynamic `new URL()` that fails to resolve is still an error. For a third-party package that can't be annotated, `turbopack.ignoreIssue` in `next.config` remains the way to suppress it.

## Verification

- `cargo nextest run -p turbopack-core -p turbopack-ecmascript -p turbopack-tests`: `snapshot/imports/ignore-comments`, which covers `turbopackIgnore` on `new Worker()`, is unchanged. 15 turbopack-core `resolve::` tests fail locally on macOS with a `/var` v
